title: How to Write a Fix and Flip Scope of Work
metaDescription: How to write a fix and flip scope of work contractors can bid accurately: structure by trade, specs, quantities, allowances, exclusions and draw-ready stages.
h1: How to Write a Fix and Flip Scope of Work Contractors Can Bid
dek: A scope of work is the written list of every task in a renovation, described specifically enough that any qualified contractor would price the same job. A biddable scope names locations, materials, quantities and standards, and states what is excluded.
keyTakeaways: A scope of work defines what will be built; the estimate prices it, and the contract and draw schedule are built from it.
Organize the scope by trade or by area, then list every task with a location, material specification, quantity and unit.
A biddable scope leaves nothing to interpretation: two contractors reading it should picture the same finished house.
Allowances, owner-supplied items and exclusions must be stated in writing, or they become disputes and change orders.
Write the scope so it can be split into draw stages tied to inspectable, completed work.

sections.h2: What is a scope of work in a fix and flip?
sections.body:
A scope of work, often abbreviated SOW, is the written description of everything a renovation will include. It lists each task, where it happens, what materials are used and to what standard it will be finished. It is the document contractors bid against, the reference you inspect against, and the backbone of the contract and the draw schedule.

It is easy to confuse the scope with the estimate. The scope says what will be done. The estimate says what it will cost. In practice the two are often combined into one document with prices beside each line, but the scope must be able to stand alone. A contractor should be able to read it, without the prices, and know exactly what you expect.

For a fix and flip, the scope also encodes your business plan. The finish level, the rooms you update and the rooms you leave alone all reflect the comps you chose and the after repair value you are targeting. When an investor and a contractor disagree halfway through a flip, the argument is almost always about something the scope did not say clearly.

A good scope protects you in several ways. It produces comparable bids. It limits change orders to genuine surprises rather than misunderstandings. It gives lenders and draw inspectors a clear basis for releasing funds. And it lets you hand the job to a project manager or a new contractor without losing the plan.

sections.h2: How should a scope of work be structured?
sections.body:
There are two common ways to organize a scope: by trade or by area. Both work, and many experienced investors combine them.

A trade-based scope groups tasks by who will do them: demolition, framing, roofing, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, insulation, drywall, flooring, cabinets and counters, tile, painting, finish carpentry, exterior and cleanup. It matches how contractors and subcontractors price work, and it makes sequencing and draw schedules straightforward.

An area-based scope groups tasks by room or zone: exterior, basement, kitchen, each bathroom, each bedroom, living areas, attic. It matches how you walked the house and how a buyer will experience it, and it makes it easy to confirm that no room was skipped.

A practical hybrid uses trades for whole-house systems and areas for finish work. For example:
- General conditions: permits, dumpster and haul-off, temporary utilities, protection of finished surfaces, final cleaning.
- Exterior: roof, gutters, siding, trim, paint, windows, doors, concrete, landscaping.
- Systems: electrical, plumbing, HVAC, water heater, sewer.
- Structure and envelope: framing repairs, foundation work, insulation, drywall.
- Rooms: kitchen, bathroom one, bathroom two, bedrooms, living areas, laundry.
- Whole-house finishes: flooring, interior paint, doors and trim, lighting package, hardware.

Number every line. Numbered lines make bids comparable, make change orders easy to reference and make draw requests precise. "Lines 4.1 through 4.9 complete" is far easier to verify than a paragraph of description.

sections.h2: What makes a scope line biddable?
sections.body:
A biddable line answers five questions: what, where, how much, with what and to what standard.

Compare two versions of the same task.

Vague: "Update bathroom."

Biddable: "Hall bath: remove existing tub surround, vanity, toilet, flooring and light fixture. Install new acrylic tub-shower surround over existing tub after reglazing tub. Replace tub-shower valve with pressure-balance valve and new trim. Install new vanity and cultured marble top, faucet, toilet, mirror and vanity light. Install tile-look LVP on floor over existing subfloor after replacing any damaged subfloor around toilet. Install ducted exhaust fan vented to exterior. Paint walls and ceiling in standard colors."

The second version can be priced by any bath contractor without a site visit, and every bidder will price roughly the same work.

The ingredients of a biddable line:
- Location: which room, which wall, which elevation.
- Action: remove, repair, replace, install, patch, refinish.
- Material specification: product type, grade or model, or a clear allowance.
- Quantity and unit: square feet, linear feet, each, squares, openings.
- Standard: what finished looks like, such as "match existing texture" or "level-four finish on kitchen walls".
- Responsibility: who supplies the material and who removes the debris.

Avoid words that mean different things to different people: "as needed", "refresh", "update", "fix", "standard". Replace each with the specific action you want.

The outline below shows the kind of detail each trade section should carry on a typical flip. Every line in your own scope should be specific to the house.

- Demolition: list each item being removed by room, note any asbestos-suspect or lead-painted materials that need testing or special handling, and state the number of dumpster loads or that haul-off is included.
- Roofing: tear-off or overlay, number of layers removed, decking replacement by sheet as needed with a stated allowance, underlayment type, shingle line and color, flashing, vents, drip edge and gutters.
- Electrical: panel replacement or retention, circuits added for kitchen and bath, GFCI and AFCI protection, device replacement throughout, fixture package by room, smoke and CO detectors, and permit and inspection.
- Plumbing: supply repipe or partial replacement and material, drain replacement, fixture rough-ins, water heater type, shutoffs, sewer camera and any lateral repair, and pressure test.
- HVAC: equipment replacement or service, duct cleaning or repair, thermostat, condensate, and permit.
- Drywall and plaster: patch locations, full replacement areas, finish level, texture match.
- Kitchen: cabinet line and layout, counter material, backsplash, sink, faucet, appliance package, hood venting.
- Bathrooms: one section per bath, as in the example above.
- Flooring: material by room, underlayment, transitions, stair treatment, baseboard and shoe.
- Paint: interior walls, ceilings, trim and doors with sheen and color; exterior surfaces with prep standard.
- Finish carpentry: doors, hardware, trim, closet systems.
- Exterior and site: siding, trim, concrete, landscaping, fence, house numbers, mailbox.
- Final: construction cleaning, punch list, rekey.

Three categories of scope language cause most disputes on flips. Handle each one in writing.

Allowances are placeholder amounts for items you have not chosen yet, such as light fixtures or tile. An allowance should state what it covers (material only, or material and installation), the quantity it applies to, and what happens if the final selection costs more or less. Too many allowances make bids hard to compare, so pick finishes before bidding whenever you can.

Owner-supplied items are materials you buy and the contractor installs, often appliances, cabinets or flooring purchased in bulk. The scope should say who receives the delivery, who checks it for damage, who stores it, who removes the packaging and what happens if items are missing or wrong. Contractors usually do not warrant materials they did not supply, and many price installation differently when they do not supply the product.

Exclusions are things that are specifically not part of the job. Listing them prevents assumptions. Common exclusions on flips include work inside walls beyond the described areas, mold or asbestos abatement, sewer line replacement beyond a stated point, appliance repair, landscaping beyond cleanup, and any area not listed in the scope. An exclusion is not a refusal to do the work. It simply means that if the work is needed, it becomes a priced change order rather than an argument.

A scope that states allowances, owner items and exclusions clearly is shorter to negotiate and much easier to manage.

sections.h2: How to handle unknowns and hidden conditions in the scope
sections.body:
No scope can see inside walls. What a scope can do is say in advance how hidden conditions will be handled.

Identify likely unknowns by name. Subfloor under tubs and toilets, framing behind water-stained drywall, wiring behind plaster, a sewer line that has not been scoped, rot at window sills, and decking under an old roof are all predictable possibilities. List them as unit-priced contingency items: "Replace damaged subfloor as found, per square foot" or "Replace roof decking as found, per sheet". This lets you approve the work quickly when it appears without negotiating from scratch.

Require discovery to be documented. Ask contractors to photograph any concealed condition before covering it or repairing it, and to submit a written change order for approval before work beyond the scope proceeds, except true emergencies such as an active leak.

Separate contingency from the base scope. Keep your contingency reserve as its own line in the budget rather than hiding it inside the trade numbers. That way you can see how much has been used and decide where it goes.

Reduce unknowns before you finalize. Turning on utilities, running every fixture, camera-scoping the sewer, pulling a few outlet covers and checking the attic all take a small amount of time and remove guesses from the scope.

On vacant and bank-owned houses, unknowns are more common, so unit-priced contingency lines matter even more.

sections.h2: Tying the scope to the draw schedule
sections.body:
A flip is usually financed with a lender who releases rehab money in draws, and even cash buyers benefit from paying contractors in stages. The scope should be written so it can be broken into draws that match completed, inspectable work.

A common sequence on a full rehab groups work into stages like these:
- Demolition complete and debris removed.
- Rough framing, rough plumbing, rough electrical and rough HVAC complete and passed inspection.
- Roof, windows and exterior envelope complete.
- Insulation and drywall complete.
- Cabinets, counters, tile and flooring installed.
- Paint, trim, fixtures and appliances complete.
- Final inspection, punch list and cleaning complete.

Each stage should list the scope line numbers it includes, so a draw inspector or lender can walk the house and confirm that every listed line is done. Avoid draw stages based on time or on a share of the contract, because they can pay for work that is not finished.

When the scope, the estimate and the draw schedule share the same numbering, everyone works from one document. Genstone Construction builds its scopes this way, with labor, materials and a draw schedule in the same estimate, so investors can see exactly which completed work each draw pays for.

sections.h2: Common scope of work mistakes on flips
sections.body:
A few mistakes appear on flip scopes again and again.

Writing the scope after getting bids. If you ask contractors to walk the house and tell you what it needs, you will get several different scopes and no way to compare prices. Write your scope first.

Leaving out general conditions. Permits, dumpsters, temporary protection, utility costs during construction and final cleaning are real costs. If they are not in the scope, some bidders will include them and others will not.

Skipping the exterior. Buyers form their first impression from the curb, and listing photos start outside. Scope landscaping cleanup, exterior paint and entry details with the same care as the kitchen.

Ignoring inspection items. Buyers' home inspectors will look at the roof, panel, water heater, HVAC, grading and safety items. A scope that addresses these up front avoids renegotiation after the buyer's inspection.

Unclear finish standards. Without a defined standard for paint coverage, drywall finish or tile layout, "done" becomes a matter of opinion.

No change order process. A scope should state how changes are requested, priced, approved and documented.

Not updating the scope. When something changes, update the document. A scope that no longer matches the job is no longer protecting you.

faqs.q: What should a fix and flip scope of work include?
faqs.a: It should include every task in the renovation organized by trade or area, each with a location, action, material specification, quantity, unit and finish standard. It should also cover general conditions such as permits, dumpsters and cleaning, list allowances and owner-supplied items, state exclusions, define how hidden conditions and change orders are handled, and group the work into draw stages tied to completed, inspectable work. Numbered lines make the document easier to bid and manage.

faqs.q: Should I write the scope or let the contractor write it?
faqs.a: Write it yourself, or have an estimator write it on your behalf, before asking for bids. When each contractor writes their own scope, you receive different plans with different prices and cannot compare them. A single scope sent to every bidder makes the numbers comparable and keeps control of the finish level and the budget with you. Contractors can still suggest changes, which you can evaluate and add to the scope for everyone.

faqs.q: How detailed does a scope of work need to be?
faqs.a: Detailed enough that a qualified contractor who has never seen the house could price it without asking questions. That usually means naming the room, the action, the material or model, the quantity and unit, and the finish standard for every line. If a line uses words like update, refresh or as needed, it is not detailed enough. More detail up front means fewer change orders and fewer disputes later.

faqs.q: How do allowances work in a renovation scope?
faqs.a: An allowance is a budgeted placeholder for an item that has not been selected yet, such as light fixtures or tile. The scope should state whether the allowance covers material only or material and installation, what quantity it applies to, and how overages or savings are handled. Allowances are useful but make bids harder to compare, so investors usually choose standard finishes before bidding and reserve allowances for a few items.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a scope of work and an estimate?
faqs.a: The scope of work describes what will be done, including tasks, locations, materials and standards. The estimate assigns costs to that work, typically with labor and material separated for each line. They are often combined into one document, but the scope must be complete on its own so contractors can bid it independently. A strong estimate is always built on a strong scope, never the other way around.
